title: Bronchiectasis Diagnosis and Management: Recurrent Infection Needs a Cause
bottomLine: Bronchiectasis is chronic abnormal bronchial dilatation with recurrent infection, sputum burden and exacerbations. Confirm the structural disease on chest CT, then look for treatable causes and build long-term airway-clearance, vaccination, microbiology and exacerbation plans rather than repeatedly treating each episode as isolated bronchitis.
recognize: Chronic daily or recurrent productive cough, recurrent lower-respiratory infections, hemoptysis, crackles and persistent sputum should raise bronchiectasis.
Frequent exacerbations or unusual airway organisms warrant a structured bronchiectasis evaluation rather than repeated empiric antibiotic courses.
differentiate: COPD and asthma can coexist with bronchiectasis but do not explain fixed bronchial dilatation on CT.
Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, immune deficiency, aspiration, prior severe infection and selected autoimmune/inflammatory diseases can be underlying causes and change management.
assessment: Characterize sputum volume/purulence, exacerbation frequency, hemoptysis, dyspnea, weight loss, aspiration risk and prior cultures.
Review childhood/recurrent infections, sinus disease, infertility clues, immune history, inflammatory disease and medication exposure.
workup: Use high-resolution chest CT to confirm bronchiectasis when clinically suspected and spirometry/full pulmonary testing to define functional impairment.

Obtain sputum culture during meaningful exacerbations and when establishing chronic microbiology; investigate etiology selectively, including immune testing, CF/PCD evaluation or aspiration assessment when the phenotype warrants it.
management: Teach an individualized airway-clearance program and optimize exercise/pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination and comorbidity treatment.
Treat exacerbations using prior/current microbiology, severity and local antimicrobial guidance rather than automatically using the same broad antibiotic every time.
Frequent exacerbations, chronic Pseudomonas or other complex infection, significant hemoptysis or progressive disease warrants respirology/bronchiectasis-clinic involvement.
medicationSafety: Long-term macrolide or inhaled antimicrobial strategies require specialist selection, interaction/QT/hearing considerations and microbiologic context; they are not default therapy for every patient.
Do not add inhaled corticosteroid solely because bronchiectasis is present unless asthma/COPD or another clear indication exists.
redFlags: Rapid functional decline or weight loss
Repeated exacerbations despite an established plan
counselling: Teach airway-clearance adherence, hydration/exercise as appropriate, vaccination and an exacerbation action plan.
Explain that identifying the underlying cause can change family counselling and long-term therapy.
followUp: Track exacerbations, cultures, symptoms, lung function and nutrition; reassess etiology when the course is atypical or rapidly progressive.
examTrap: Treating the fifth productive-cough episode as another simple bronchitis without recognizing chronic sputum, recurrent infection and CT-confirmed structural airway disease.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiectasis care is airway clearance plus microbiology plus cause—not antibiotics alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Non-CF Bronchiectasis Assembly and respiratory practice resources

title: Pulmonary Hypertension Recognition and Referral: Find the Group Before the Drug
bottomLine: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic syndrome with multiple causes. Unexplained exertional dyspnea, syncope, right-heart findings or suggestive echocardiography should trigger cause-directed evaluation and specialty referral; pulmonary arterial hypertension drugs should not be started simply because an echocardiogram estimates elevated pulmonary pressure.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pressure, exertional syncope/presyncope, edema, elevated JVP and a loud P2 can signal advanced pulmonary vascular/right-heart disease.
Systemic sclerosis, congenital heart disease, chronic thromboembolic disease, portal hypertension, HIV and selected drugs/exposures raise specific pulmonary arterial hypertension risk.
differentiate: Pulmonary hypertension due to left-heart disease or chronic lung/hypoxic disease is more common than idiopathic PAH and is managed by treating the underlying condition rather than reflex PAH-targeted therapy.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension is potentially intervention-treatable and must not be missed in a patient with persistent dyspnea after PE.
assessment: Assess functional limitation, exertional syncope, edema, hypoxemia, VTE history, connective-tissue disease, congenital disease, liver disease, sleep/lung disease and medication/toxin exposure.
Examine for right-heart failure and clues to left-heart, lung or systemic causes.
workup: Use ECG, chest imaging, oxygenation, PFTs and echocardiography as part of the initial cause-directed evaluation; test for thromboembolic/systemic causes according to phenotype.
Right-heart catheterization is required to establish the hemodynamic diagnosis/classification before PAH-specific treatment decisions in specialty care.
management: Refer suspected clinically significant pulmonary hypertension to an experienced pulmonary vascular/cardiology-respirology pathway.
Treat contributing left-heart, lung, hypoxemia, sleep-disordered breathing or thromboembolic disease and use diuretics cautiously for right-sided congestion when appropriate.
Pregnancy in established pulmonary arterial hypertension is very high risk and requires urgent expert multidisciplinary management.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe PAH-targeted vasodilator therapy from an elevated echocardiographic pressure estimate alone; treatment depends on hemodynamic group and expert assessment.
Review hypotension, interactions and pregnancy risks before any pulmonary vascular therapy.
redFlags: Suspected chronic thromboembolic PH with deterioration
counselling: Explain that 'pulmonary hypertension' describes pressure/hemodynamics, while identifying the cause determines treatment.
Provide clear activity and emergency-return guidance when syncope or right-heart failure risk is present.
followUp: Close the loop on specialty referral and required hemodynamic/cause testing; worsening functional class requires expedited reassessment.
examTrap: Starting a PAH-specific drug after an echocardiogram reports elevated pulmonary pressure without determining whether the patient has left-heart, lung, thromboembolic or true precapillary pulmonary vascular disease.
oneLinePearl: Pulmonary hypertension is classified before it is treated.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Thoracic Society Pulmonary Hypertension Position Statement

title: Sarcoidosis Diagnosis and Management: Granulomas Need Context
bottomLine: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous diagnosis that requires a compatible clinical-radiographic syndrome, exclusion of important mimics and tissue confirmation when the diagnosis is uncertain or treatment would carry meaningful risk. Not every radiographic abnormality needs corticosteroids.
recognize: Bilateral hilar/mediastinal adenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, dry cough and dyspnea are common thoracic patterns.
Eye, skin, cardiac, neurologic, calcium, liver and constitutional manifestations can be more important than the chest symptoms.
differentiate: Tuberculosis, fungal infection, lymphoma, occupational/environmental granulomatous disease and drug reactions can mimic sarcoidosis.
Asymptomatic/stable pulmonary sarcoidosis differs from organ-threatening cardiac, neurologic, ocular or progressive pulmonary disease.
assessment: Assess respiratory symptoms plus visual complaints, palpitations/syncope, neurologic symptoms, skin lesions, calcium-stone symptoms, constitutional features and occupational/infectious exposure risk.
workup: Use chest imaging and pulmonary function testing to define thoracic disease; obtain ECG and organ-directed testing based on symptoms/risk.
Biopsy the safest informative site when tissue confirmation is needed, and exclude relevant infection/malignancy before immunosuppression.
management: Observe selected mild/stable disease with planned monitoring rather than treating imaging alone.

Use specialist-directed corticosteroid or steroid-sparing therapy for symptomatic progressive or organ-threatening disease, with organ-specific referral for cardiac, ocular, neurologic or other high-risk involvement.
medicationSafety: Before meaningful immunosuppression, review infection risks, vaccination and drug-specific laboratory/organ monitoring.
Do not escalate corticosteroids for presumed sarcoidosis before reconsidering infection when fever, new infiltrates or immunosuppression complicates the picture.
redFlags: Syncope or ventricular arrhythmia/cardiac involvement concern
counselling: Explain that sarcoidosis can involve organs beyond the lungs and that treatment depends on symptoms and organ risk, not radiograph stage alone.
followUp: Track symptoms, pulmonary function and organ-specific disease; re-evaluate diagnosis when the course is atypical or treatment response is poor.
examTrap: Giving prolonged corticosteroids solely because bilateral hilar adenopathy is present without assessing symptoms, dangerous organ involvement or infectious/malignant mimics.
oneLinePearl: Sarcoidosis is treated for organ risk and symptoms—not for an X-ray alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Interstitial Lung Disease Assembly and guideline resources

title: Cystic Fibrosis Adult Management Basics: Chronic Disease, Rapid Exacerbation Decisions
bottomLine: Adults with cystic fibrosis require specialized multidisciplinary longitudinal care. Outside the CF clinic, the NP's job is to recognize pulmonary exacerbation or CF-related complications early, preserve the patient's established airway-clearance/medication plan when safe, obtain meaningful cultures and coordinate promptly with the CF team rather than treating CF as ordinary bronchitis or COPD.
recognize: Increased cough/sputum, change in sputum character, dyspnea, fatigue, appetite/weight loss and declining lung function can signal pulmonary exacerbation.
CF is multisystem: pancreatic insufficiency, CF-related diabetes, liver disease, bone disease, fertility/pregnancy and mental health all affect care.
differentiate: A pulmonary exacerbation may be present without fever and may involve chronic airway organisms requiring individualized antimicrobial selection.
Hemoptysis, pneumothorax, distal intestinal obstruction and severe hyperglycemia are distinct complications that require their own acute pathways.
assessment: Compare symptoms to the patient's baseline and review prior airway microbiology, CFTR modulator therapy, airway-clearance regimen, nutrition/weight, diabetes, oxygenation and recent antibiotic history.
Ask which CF centre follows the patient and obtain the current care plan when possible.
workup: For suspected pulmonary exacerbation, obtain respiratory culture when feasible and use chest imaging/labs according to severity; interpret spirometry change against baseline rather than population normal alone.
Screen other CF complications according to the established CF program rather than creating an ad hoc general-primary-care schedule.
management: Contact the CF team early for a meaningful exacerbation, especially with declining lung function, hypoxemia, hemoptysis or prior resistant organisms.
Continue airway clearance and chronic therapies when clinically appropriate; antimicrobial route/choice/duration depends on severity, prior microbiology and specialist plan.
Use current Canadian CF standards for CFTR modulators and multidisciplinary monitoring.
medicationSafety: CFTR modulators have genotype eligibility, drug-interaction and organ-monitoring requirements; do not start/stop them casually outside the treatment plan.
Repeated antibiotics require review of prior cultures, renal/hepatic function and cumulative toxicity.
counselling: Reinforce CF-centre follow-up and adherence without blaming patients for high treatment burden.
Discuss infection-prevention practices and individualized exercise/nutrition plans from the CF team.
followUp: Ensure CF-centre review after acute care and close the loop on culture results, antibiotics and recovery to baseline.
examTrap: Treating an adult with CF and worsening productive cough using a routine community-acquired bronchitis prescription without checking prior airway cultures or contacting the CF program.
oneLinePearl: In CF, baseline microbiology and the CF team's plan are part of the vital signs.
sourceBasis: Cystic Fibrosis Canada — Canadian Guidelines for Cystic Fibrosis Care
Cystic Fibrosis Canada guideline for pulmonary exacerbations
Cystic Fibrosis Canada CFTR modulator consensus guidance

title: Respiratory Infection in the Immunocompromised Host: Broaden the Differential, Lower the Threshold
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients can have severe respiratory infection with muted fever, leukocytosis or examination findings. Define the immune defect, exposure and illness tempo early, assess oxygenation and organ dysfunction, and escalate diagnostic/treatment intensity before deterioration makes the pathogen obvious.
recognize: Risk depends on the type and intensity of immunosuppression: neutropenia, transplant, B-cell/T-cell suppression, corticosteroids/biologics and advanced hematologic disease create different pathogen spectra.
Hypoxemia, tachypnea, altered mentation or rapid radiographic progression can precede dramatic fever/inflammatory markers.
differentiate: Routine community respiratory viruses/bacteria remain possible, but opportunistic fungal, Pneumocystis, mycobacterial and reactivation infections enter the differential according to the immune defect and prophylaxis.
Drug-induced pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage and malignancy can mimic infection in immunocompromised patients.
assessment: Document the underlying disease, transplant status, neutrophil/lymphocyte context, immunosuppressive agents, prophylaxis, vaccination, prior pathogens/resistance, recent hospitalization/travel/exposures and oxygenation.
Assess severity first; apparently mild cough in a highly immunocompromised host can be high risk.
workup: Use chest imaging early when lower-respiratory disease is plausible and obtain targeted viral/microbiologic testing based on host risk and severity.
CBC/differential, renal/hepatic function, blood cultures and specialty sampling such as bronchoscopy are selected according to immune defect and clinical instability rather than a universal panel.
management: Escalate unstable, hypoxemic, neutropenic or rapidly progressive illness to acute/infectious-disease care and initiate empiric therapy according to syndrome, immune defect and local resistance guidance without waiting for every final result.
Use isolation and current respiratory-virus prevention/treatment pathways and coordinate with oncology/transplant/immunology teams.
medicationSafety: Antimicrobial choices require interaction and organ-function review because azoles, macrolides, antivirals and immunosuppressants commonly interact.
Do not stop essential immunosuppression reflexively; coordinate changes with the responsible specialty unless an immediate life-threatening reaction requires emergency action.
redFlags: Hypoxemia or rapidly rising oxygen need
counselling: Teach early reporting of respiratory symptoms and current vaccination/infection-prevention measures; immunocompromised patients may qualify for additional seasonal vaccine doses or other prevention strategies.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures/PCR, antimicrobial changes and specialty follow-up; persistent symptoms require reconsideration of opportunistic infection and noninfectious mimics.
examTrap: Reassuring a severely immunocompromised patient because fever and WBC are normal despite new hypoxemia and progressive respiratory symptoms.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, normal inflammation does not equal low risk.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada respiratory infectious-disease guidance for high-risk/immunocompromised persons
Canadian Thoracic Society infection-screening guidance for immunosuppression

title: Thoracentesis Indications and Complications: Sample or Drain With a Question
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is performed to answer a diagnostic question or relieve a clinically significant effusion—not because pleural fluid merely exists. Confirm the indication, use ultrasound/local procedural standards, collect the specimens that answer the differential, and reassess immediately for pneumothorax, bleeding or respiratory deterioration.
recognize: Unexplained unilateral effusion, suspected infection/malignancy and atypical effusion despite presumed heart failure commonly create a diagnostic indication.
Large symptomatic effusions may need therapeutic drainage even when the etiology is already known.
differentiate: A classic bilateral heart-failure effusion improving with treatment may not need immediate diagnostic sampling.
Pleural infection/empyema is not managed by a one-time diagnostic tap alone when drainage criteria are met.
assessment: Confirm symptoms, oxygenation, imaging, laterality/size, suspected cause, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, bleeding history and ability to cooperate/position safely.
Know which studies are needed before the procedure so fluid is collected/handled correctly.
workup: Use bedside/diagnostic ultrasound to identify fluid and a safe site in accordance with local procedural standards.
Send pleural protein/LDH and other tests such as cell count, pH, glucose, Gram/culture, cytology or targeted testing only when they answer the differential.
management: Perform the procedure within training, credentialing and local policy; monitor symptoms and vital signs during/after drainage.
Escalate suspected complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema, hemothorax or malignant/recurrent effusion to the appropriate drainage/specialty pathway.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic management around thoracentesis is indication-, agent-, urgency- and local-protocol dependent; do not apply a universal hold interval.
Avoid indiscriminate large-volume rapid drainage when symptoms suggest re-expansion or hemodynamic intolerance; follow local technique/protocol.
counselling: Explain whether the goal is diagnosis, symptom relief or both and what complications should be reported immediately.
followUp: Review pleural-fluid results and imaging until etiology is resolved; do not let a successful drain become a lost diagnostic follow-up.
examTrap: Ordering or performing thoracentesis simply because an effusion is visible without asking whether the procedure will change diagnosis or relieve clinically important symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Thoracentesis needs a question, a safe site and a plan for the answer.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Chest Procedures Assembly practice resources
Canadian pleural-disease and ultrasound-guided procedure practice standards

title: Mechanical Ventilation Basics for NP: Treat the Patient, Read the Ventilator
bottomLine: Mechanical ventilation is organ support, not treatment of the underlying disease. When a ventilated patient deteriorates, assess the patient and airway first, then determine whether the problem is oxygenation, ventilation, mechanics, equipment or the underlying illness; do not respond to every alarm by simply increasing settings.
recognize: FiO2/PEEP mainly influence oxygenation; minute ventilation is driven by tidal volume and respiratory rate and affects CO2 clearance.
Peak pressure can rise from airway resistance or reduced compliance, while plateau pressure more directly reflects static respiratory-system pressure/compliance when measured correctly.
differentiate: Sudden high-pressure alarm may reflect kinked/blocked tube, biting, bronchospasm, secretions, pneumothorax or worsening compliance.
Sudden low pressure/volume may indicate disconnection or cuff/circuit leak; a deteriorating patient requires immediate bedside evaluation rather than remote alarm silencing.
assessment: Check patient appearance, oxygenation, hemodynamics, chest movement, airway/tube position, breath sounds and synchrony before interpreting the ventilator display.
Review the ventilator mode/settings, measured tidal/minute volumes, pressures and recent ABG/gas trend in context of the disease.
workup: Use ABG/venous gas where appropriate, chest imaging, ECG/labs and bedside ultrasound according to the suspected problem.
If equipment failure or tube obstruction is suspected in an unstable patient, follow the emergency airway/ventilator troubleshooting pathway and manually ventilate when indicated while help arrives.
management: Use lung-protective ventilation principles for patients at risk of ventilator-induced lung injury and titrate oxygen/PEEP/ventilation to the clinical target rather than normalizing every gas value.
Treat causes such as bronchospasm, secretions, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, sepsis or agitation/dyssynchrony and coordinate with respiratory therapy/critical care.
Long-term non-invasive ventilation/home ventilation decisions require disease-specific specialist criteria.
medicationSafety: Sedation, analgesia and neuromuscular blockade have hemodynamic/delirium/weakness risks and require explicit indications and monitoring.
Avoid unnecessary deep sedation when a lighter target is safe; do not paralyze a patient without adequate sedation/analgesia.
redFlags: Absent unilateral breath sounds with rising pressure
counselling: When appropriate, explain the goals of ventilation and weaning to the patient/family and distinguish temporary organ support from prognosis.
followUp: Reassess gas exchange, mechanics, sedation, spontaneous-breathing/weaning readiness and the underlying disease each day in critical care.
examTrap: Responding to a high-pressure alarm by increasing pressure limits without first checking the patient, tube, secretions, bronchospasm and pneumothorax.
oneLinePearl: Ventilator alarm plus deterioration: patient first, circuit second, numbers third.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society mechanical-ventilation guideline library

title: Asthma-COPD Overlap Syndrome Management: Treat the Traits, Protect Against Asthma Risk
bottomLine: Patients can have persistent COPD-type obstruction plus convincing asthma features. Confirm obstruction/variability, define exacerbation risk and treat the dominant traits; when asthma is truly present, an inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimen is part of safety and LABA monotherapy should not be used as asthma treatment.
recognize: Earlier-life variable symptoms, atopy/eosinophilic features and marked reversibility support asthma traits, while smoking/exposure history and persistent post-bronchodilator obstruction support COPD traits.
Do not use 'overlap' as a substitute for objective spirometry and a real disease history.
differentiate: Asthma and COPD remain distinct diagnoses with overlapping phenotypes rather than one universally defined syndrome.
Heart failure, bronchiectasis, vocal-cord dysfunction, obesity/deconditioning and ILD can mimic mixed obstructive symptoms.
assessment: Assess age at symptom onset, variability, triggers/atopy, smoking/occupational exposure, exacerbations/hospitalizations, eosinophilic clues, inhaler technique, adherence and comorbidity.
Review prior spirometry and response to therapy rather than diagnosing from labels in the chart.
workup: Use spirometry with bronchodilator assessment to confirm persistent obstruction and evidence of variability when present.
Additional eosinophil/allergy testing or imaging is selected when it changes phenotype/therapy or another diagnosis is suspected.
management: Ensure an ICS-containing strategy when the patient has convincing asthma, then add long-acting bronchodilator therapy according to persistent symptoms/exacerbation risk and current asthma/COPD guidance.
Smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation/exercise, inhaler technique and action planning are core disease-modifying supports.
Frequent exacerbations despite optimized treatment should trigger phenotype review, adherence/technique assessment and specialist referral rather than indefinite inhaler stacking.
medicationSafety: LABA monotherapy is not appropriate asthma treatment; asthma risk must be protected with ICS-containing therapy.

Higher/intensive ICS exposure can increase pneumonia and other adverse effects in COPD-predominant patients, so use the lowest effective regimen consistent with asthma safety and exacerbation control.
counselling: Teach the purpose of each inhaler and why the regimen may differ from a patient with only asthma or only COPD.
Use a written action plan and verify device technique at follow-up.
followUp: Track symptoms, exacerbations, spirometry, pneumonia/ICS adverse effects, smoking status and inhaler use; reassess the diagnosis if the course does not fit.
examTrap: Calling a smoker with wheeze 'COPD only' and using LABA without ICS despite a clear prior asthma history and variable airflow symptoms.
oneLinePearl: When asthma is truly present inside chronic obstruction, preserve asthma-safe anti-inflammatory therapy while treating COPD traits.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current asthma guideline resources
Canadian Thoracic Society current COPD pharmacotherapy guideline
